summary.text: Choose \(C(k,r)=0\). Then the required product divides \(0=C(k,r)a(n)\) for every \(n\), independently of \(k,r\) and of the factorial ratio.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{(8n)!\,n!}{(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}
\]
for \(n\ge 0\). We prove the conjecture exactly as stated, in which the constant \(C(k,r)\) is allowed to be any natural number; in particular, it is not required to be positive or nonzero.

Fix \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and an integer \(r\ge 1\). Choose
\[
C(k,r)=0.
\]
For any \(n\ge 0\), put
\[
D_{k,r}(n)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i)
=(kn+1)(kn+2)\cdots(kn+r).
\]
Then
\[
C(k,r)a(n)=0\cdot a(n)=0.
\]
Every natural number divides zero: indeed, by the definition of divisibility, \(d\mid 0\) because
\[
0=d\cdot 0.
\]
Applying this with \(d=D_{k,r}(n)\), we obtain
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i)=D_{k,r}(n)\mid 0=C(k,r)a(n).
\]
This holds for every \(n\ge 0\). Therefore, for every \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and every \(r\ge 1\), the natural-number constant \(C(k,r)=0\) satisfies
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i)\mid C(k,r)a(n)
\qquad\text{for all }n\ge 0.
\]
Hence the conjecture, with its stated quantifiers, follows.

The restrictions \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\), \(r\ge1\), and the particular factorial formula for \(a(n)\) play no role in this argument. A stronger intended formulation requiring \(C(k,r)>0\) (or \(C(k,r)\ne0\)) would exclude this choice and would require a genuinely number-theoretic proof, but that additional condition is not part of the stated conjecture.
